background.definition: Anal fissure is a linear tear in the anoderm, usually from the dentate line to the anal verge. Chronic fissure is usually present for at least 6 to 8 weeks and is more commonly characterized by extension through the submucosa exposing fibers of the internal anal sphincter (IAS), perianal skin tag (or "sentinel pile"), and hypertrophied anal papilla.

list.listitem: Common, but actual incidence unknown; affects about 10% of patients attending colorectal clinics.
Both sexes are affected equally; however, women have posterior, rectovaginal fissures and men have complications from anorectal abcesses.
It is more common in young to middle-aged adults, with 87% occurring in patients between the ages of 20 and 60 years.
Most common cause of rectal bleeding in infancy.
Acute: mechanical force generated by passage of large hard stool through an anal canal too small to accommodate it.
Diarrhea with anal mucosal irritation (4%-7%).
Fissures with atypical features (eg, multiple, off midline) can be caused by inflammatory bowel disease, local or systemic malignancy, venereal infection, trauma, tuberculosis, or chemotherapy.

Exact mechanism is unknown. There is an association of anal fissure with sphincter hypertonia; internal anal sphincter tone, as measured by anal manometry, is elevated in patients with anal fissures versus controls.
Relative lack of nitric oxide synthase has been suggested as a possible mechanism for internal anal sphincter hypertonia.
It is postulated that spasm also gives rise to ischemia, causing pain and leading to chronicity.
Prevention is a diet high in fiber and proper toileting to avoid constipation and straining. C
Patients typically present with pain on defecation and intermittent minor bright red rectal bleeding; a fissure is identified on examination. C
The diagnosis of anal fissure is made clinically; no diagnostic tests are necessary. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Usually less painful (unless thrombosed), soft palpable mass

list.listitem: Patients may complain of sharp or severe rectal pain during and after defecation lasting several hours, bright red bleeding, or less commonly constipation (reported in about 20%; about equal to the general population) or chronic diarrhea (4%-7%).
Obtain a history to rule out red flags for more serious illness (anemia, weight loss, fever, history of malignancy, and signs of perforation or obstruction).

Visual examination of the rectum may detect the fissure (acute); in chronic fissure visual examination of the rectum reveals anal skin tag(s) associated with the fissure and visible muscle fibers or granulation tissue.
Gentle physical examination (without digital rectal examination) reveals the fissure. More than 90% of fissures are posterior and midline.
Significant pain may require examination under anesthesia.

Atypical features include non-midline, multiple, and elderly patient; in these cases, evaluation for an underlying etiology is warranted. Further examination in these cases can reveal arthritis, (ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease,) dermatologic findings (erythema nodosum, pyogenic granuloma), pulmonary findings (TB), or genital findings (syphilis).
There are no specific diagnostic tests for anal fissures.

Rule out malignancy with colonoscopy and other studies as indicated in patients with red flags (ie, older than 40 years, anemia, weight loss, fever, history of malignancy, signs of perforation or obstruction).
See for a suggested approach to management.
Identification of fissure does not preclude colorectal malignancy; strongly consider colonoscopy in patients older than 40 years and in every patient with red flags for malignancy.

For acute and chronic anal fissures, consider initial medical therapy using using topical nitrate, topical calcium channel blocker (nifedipine or diltiazem), and topical tocopherol acetate (vitamin E); second-line medical therapy includes Botulinum toxin (Botox) injection. B
For chronic anal fissure refractory to medical management, internal sphincterotomy is most effective. Open and closed partial lateral internal sphincterotomy appear similarly effective. B

Nitroglycerin ointment (glycerol trinitrate 0.2%-0.4%), made by a compounding pharmacist, reduces anal canal resting pressure and promotes healing. It is only marginally better, however, than placebo (48.9% healing vs. 35.5%). Common side effects are headache and postural hypotension. A small, single-blinded RCT found that endoanal application of nitroglycerin was associated with fewer and less severe headaches compared with perianal application.

Other potentially useful medications are topical calcium channel blockers (which would have to be made by a compounding pharmacist in the United States) and Botulinum toxin (Botox). One RCT of 100 patients randomized them to botox or placebo and found a lower failure rate with active treatment (NNT = 5). A systematic review of 18 trials (n = 1158) concluded that lower doses of botox were as effective as higher doses, and associated with lower incontinence and recurrence rates.

In a Cochrane review, topical calcium channel blockers (nifedipine and diltiazem) and Botox were found to be as effective as nitroglycerine, with fewer adverse effects. In one retrospective study, the combination of topical nifedipine and Botox was superior to nitroglycerin and pneumatic dilation, with improved healing (94% vs. 71%, NNT = 5) and lower recurrence rates (2% vs. 27%, NNT = 4).

Repeat topical treatments can be tried after 6 to 8 weeks if anal fissure persists. Efficacy of repeating treatments is case by case, as it is unknown who will need a repeat treatment upon starting the first treatment.
For chronic fissures, the use of topical nifedipine and lidocaine was more effective than topical lidocaine and hydrocortisone ointment (94.5% healing by 6 weeks vs. 16.4%; NNT = 1.3).
In 1 study of chronic fissures, Botox was slightly more effective than topical nitroglycerine, with 92% versus 70% healing at the end of 8 weeks (NNT = 5; 95% CI, 3-16).

Based on 1 RCT involving 160 adults, tocopherol acetate (vitamin E) ointment appears more effective in eliminating pain in patients with chronic anal fissure compared to glyceryl trinitrate ointment at 8 weeks (87.5% vs 70%, NNT = 6), reducing mean anal pain (mean difference 10.9 mm on visual analogue scale of 1-100 mm; 4.3-18.6), decreasing recurrence at 24 weeks (2.9% vs 13.2%), and has less adverse effects (0 vs 14 patients reporting severe headache leading to withdrawal from glyceryl trinitrate ointment). However, these findings may be an overestimate of the true effect of vitamin E ointment since patients were not masked to the treatment group assignment.

The presence of fissure for more than 12 months, anal tags, persistently elevated manometric mean pressure, and increased percentage of time of ultraslow waves is associated with higher recurrence rates. These patients may be candidates for surgical intervention as the initial therapeutic choice.

For chronic anal fissure, options include partial internal anal sphincterotomy, anal dilation, and surgical flap. In a Cochrane review of 27 trials, anal stretch had a higher risk of fissure persistence and minor incontinence than internal sphincterotomy. There were no differences between open and closed partial lateral internal anal sphincterotomy.
For acute anal fissure, stool softeners (ie, bran 15 g daily) are recommended for those with constipation.

Sitz baths are superior to not having other treatments such as lidocaine ointment or hydrocortisone ointment. A systematic review concluded that the current evidence does not support the value of sitz baths for anorectal disorders.
Recurrent or chronic fistula requires referral for surgery.
About half of patients will heal with conservative management, but about 25% of these will have a recurrence within 5 years. B
Results are generally good after surgery. B

cell.label: Uncomplicated anal fissure without history of Crohn's or HIV. Rule out malignancy if red flags.
Trial of topical nitroglycerine or calcium channel blocker. Increase water and fiber, consider Sitz baths, use analgesics. Healed at 6 to 8 weeks?
Second course of topical therapy (nitroglycerin or calcium channel blocker). Treatment failure?
Consider lateral internal sphincterotomy or fissurectomy, and further diagnostic testing.
